title: Battery Point Terrace: Waterproof Hybrid Restoration
summary: Heritage proportions kept intact with a waterproof hybrid floor that runs unbroken through a listed terrace.

hero.alt: Warm oak-look hybrid planks running through the open living space of a restored Battery Point terrace.

challenge.heading: The Challenge & Vision
challenge.body: An 1880s terrace with original skirtings the owners would not part with, and a subfloor that had settled more than 20mm across the length of the hallway. The brief was a single unbroken floor from the front door through to the rear extension, waterproof enough for a bathroom threshold, and installed without lifting a single piece of heritage joinery.

image.alt: Original skirting boards masked off ahead of levelling work in a heritage terrace.

solution.heading: The Solution
solution.body: We mapped the settlement with a laser level and brought the whole floor to plane with a fibre-reinforced levelling compound poured in three stages. A 6mm hybrid plank in a soft smoked oak went down floating over acoustic underlay, scribed to the existing skirtings rather than butted against new quad — the detail that keeps the room reading as original.

image.alt: Smoked oak hybrid planks scribed neatly against original heritage skirting.

challenge.heading: The Challenge & Vision
challenge.body: A waterfront room that swings from damp winter mornings to a full house on a summer evening, with the humidity range that implies. Solid timber would have cupped within a season. The owners still wanted a real oak surface underfoot in the dining room, and the fitout window was the ten days between Christmas and the January trade.

We needed a floor that could be cleaned to clinical standard, and a programme that never took more than one room out of service at a time.

summary: An engineered oak herringbone set out from the room's sightline rather than its walls, which are not square.

hero.alt: Herringbone engineered timber laid through a naturally lit waterfront gallery space.

challenge.heading: The Challenge & Vision
challenge.body: A converted warehouse where no two walls are parallel and the fall across the slab is 40mm. Herringbone shows every setting-out error, and a gallery lit from above shows every high spot as a shadow. The pattern had to look deliberate from the entry, which meant ignoring the walls entirely.

image.alt: Herringbone blocks being dry-laid to establish the setting-out line.

seo.metaDescription: Engineered oak herringbone laid in a Hobart waterfront gallery, set out from the entry sightline because none of the heritage walls run square.

cta.heading: Inspired by this project?
cta.description: Tell us about your space and we will walk you through the options, the timeline and the cost.

solution.heading: The Solution
solution.body: We set the pattern out from the sightline through the entry doors, not from any wall, and absorbed the out-of-square into a wide border block at the perimeter. The slab was levelled to a 2mm tolerance over three metres before a single block went down — tighter than the code calls for, because raking gallery light is unforgiving.

image.alt: Perimeter border blocks absorbing the out-of-square at a gallery wall.

challenge.heading: The Challenge & Vision
challenge.body: The body corporate had knocked back a previous flooring proposal on acoustic grounds, and the by-laws set a hard impact-sound limit for any hard floor above ground level. Six apartments needed the same specification, documented well enough to be approved once rather than argued unit by unit.

image.alt: Acoustic underlay laid out across an apartment floor before planking.

solution.heading: The Solution
solution.body: We built a single specification around a 6mm hybrid plank over a 3mm high-density rubber acoustic mat, tested as a system rather than as two products. Perimeter isolation strips keep the floor from bridging to the wall structure — the detail most floating floors miss, and the usual reason an impact test fails.

image.alt: High-density acoustic mat with perimeter isolation strips fitted at the wall.

items.title: Perimeter Isolation
items.description: No rigid bridge between floor and wall — the usual cause of a failed test.

challenge.heading: The Challenge & Vision
challenge.body: A heritage-listed homestead where the floor structure had failed but the surface could not simply be replaced. Consent required that original material be retained wherever it was sound, and that anything new be period-appropriate in species, width and finish. Every board had to be accounted for.

image.alt: Original homestead boards lifted and numbered ahead of structural repairs.

cta.heading: Inspired by this project?

solution.heading: The Solution
solution.body: We lifted and numbered the entire floor, repaired the joists beneath, then relaid every sound original board in its recorded position. Gaps were filled with reclaimed stock of the same period sourced from a demolition in the Midlands. The finish is a traditional hardwax oil — reversible, repairable, and acceptable to the heritage assessor in a way a modern polyurethane would not have been.

challenge.heading: The Challenge & Vision
challenge.body: Under the carpet were the original boards — along with a century of tack holes, two failed patches in pine, and a band of paint where a wall had been removed. The owners wanted the floor to read as old without reading as damaged, which is a much finer line than a full replacement.

image.alt: Original cottage boards exposed after carpet removal, showing tack holes and paint.

seo.metaTitle: West Hobart Cottage Timber Floor Restoration
seo.metaDescription: Original Tasmanian Oak boards in a West Hobart cottage stripped, patched with salvaged stock and re-finished in a low-sheen hardwax oil.

cta.heading: Inspired by this project?
cta.description: Tell us about your space and we will walk you through the options, the timeline and the cost.

solution.heading: The Solution
solution.body: The pine patches came out and were replaced with salvaged Tasmanian Oak of the same period and width, laid to match the existing board runs. We sanded through three grits, filled the tack holes with a matched slurry rather than a uniform filler, and finished in a low-sheen hardwax oil that can be spot-repaired in future without recoating the whole room.

image.alt: Salvaged Tasmanian Oak boards let into the original floor and sanded flush.
